name: Haudenosaunee White Corn Soup — Home Adaptation
imageAlt: Illustrative white corn; this photograph is not identified as a Haudenosaunee white corn cultivar
imageCredit: Photo: Willis Lam, Wikimedia Commons/Flickr, CC BY-SA 2.0. Image illustrates white corn generally and is not presented as a verified Haudenosaunee cultivar.
summary: A carefully framed home version of Haudenosaunee white corn soup with prepared hulled corn, beans and beef, based on publicly shared Mohawk and Seneca recipes.
lead: Prepared white corn, beans and meat simmer together for hours in a soup whose importance reaches far beyond its short ingredient list.
about: White corn soup is a deeply important Haudenosaunee food with distinct nation, community and family versions. Public Mohawk and Seneca recipes commonly combine specially prepared white corn with beans and meat. This page deliberately starts with already hulled, food-ready Haudenosaunee white corn so it does not turn the culturally significant hardwood-ash preparation process into a casual shortcut tutorial.
story: Onondaga Nation describes Onehogwa', corn soup, as a food served within community life and ceremony and emphasizes the importance of white corn grown among Haudenosaunee communities. First Nations Health Authority publishes Akwesasne Mohawk cook Richard Jock's family corn-soup recipe and explicitly notes the friendly rivalries among Iroquois communities over beans, vegetables and other additions. Cornell's Traditional Iroquois Corn guide documents a Seneca preparation from Tonawanda. Together, these sources make clear that there is no single generic 'Iroquois soup' formula.
caveat: This home adaptation assumes you have purchased properly prepared hulled Haudenosaunee white corn from an appropriate food source. It intentionally does not reproduce ceremonial context or provide casual hardwood-ash processing instructions.
prepNotes: Start with food-ready hulled white corn
Do not substitute ordinary canned sweet corn and do not improvise lye or ash processing without community-grounded instruction.
Cook the meat until yielding
The long simmer builds the broth and should leave the beef easy to pull apart.
Expect community variation
Kidney beans, white beans, turnip, onion, pork, venison and beef all appear in publicly shared versions; this is one practical pathway.
ingredients: 3 cups cooked or food-ready hulled Haudenosaunee white corn
1 1/2 lb beef chuck or venison, cut into 1-inch pieces
1 cup dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight and drained
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
steps: Combine meat and water in a large heavy pot. Bring to a boil, skim foam if desired, then reduce to a gentle simmer for 1 1/2 hours.
Add soaked beans and turnip. Continue simmering about 1 hour, adding hot water if the solids rise above the broth.
Add onion and cook 20 minutes.
Add the prepared hulled white corn and continue simmering 30–45 minutes.
Checkpoint: beans should be creamy inside, meat should pull apart easily and the prepared corn should be tender and swollen while still recognizable.
Season with salt only after the long simmer, since evaporation concentrates the broth.
Rest 10 minutes before serving. The soup should be substantial and corn-forward rather than heavily spiced.
sources: First Nations Health Authority — Food is Medicine: Mohawk Corn and Corn Soup
Cornell University — Traditional Iroquois Corn, including a Seneca corn-soup recipe
Onondaga Nation — Corn Soup Dinner and community context

name: Sudanese Kisra
imageAlt: Thin sheets of Sudanese kisra made from fermented sorghum batter
imageCredit: Photo: Marwa Siddig Aljally Altaueb, Wikimedia Commons, CC0 1.0
summary: Sudanese kisra: a tangy fermented sorghum batter spread paper-thin on a hot griddle and served with mullah stews.
lead: Fermented sorghum batter becomes impossibly thin, flexible bread on a hot griddle—a Sudanese staple designed to meet stew.
about: Kisra is a Sudanese fermented sorghum flatbread cooked in very thin sheets on a hot griddle. The batter is fermented until mildly sour, diluted to a flowing consistency, then spread rapidly so the bread sets almost immediately. It is traditionally paired with mullah stews and functions as a staple rather than an occasional specialty.
story: Sudan's embassy describes kisra as a major national staple made from durra, or sorghum. Archaeological and food-science research traces sorghum flatbread traditions deep into Sudanese history and documents the distinctive fermented batter and hot doka or saj cooking surface. Contemporary Sudanese cooks still describe the spreading technique as the difficult part: a good sheet is extremely thin, soft and tangy rather than pancake-thick.
caveat: Traditional kisra technique uses specialized griddles and spreading tools and takes practice. This nonstick-skillet adaptation preserves sorghum fermentation and one-sided thin cooking while acknowledging that the shaping technique is simplified.
prepNotes: Ferment until tangy
The batter should smell pleasantly sour before cooking; an unfermented batter misses a defining part of kisra.
Thin after fermentation
Ferment a somewhat thicker mixture first, then dilute until it flows easily across the pan.
Cook only one side
Kisra is spread very thin and traditionally lifts once the upper surface dries; flipping is unnecessary when the batter is thin enough.
ingredients: 2 cups lukewarm water for the initial batter, plus 1 to 2 cups more after fermentation
2 tbsp plain yogurt or 1/4 cup active kisra starter, optional but helpful
Neutral oil, for wiping the pan
steps: Whisk sorghum flour with 2 cups lukewarm water and yogurt or starter if using until smooth and thickly pourable.
Cover loosely and leave at room temperature 12–24 hours, depending on room temperature and starter strength.
Checkpoint: the batter should smell distinctly but pleasantly sour and show small bubbles or other signs of fermentation.
Whisk in salt and enough additional water to make a very thin batter, looser than American pancake batter.
Heat a large nonstick skillet or flat griddle over medium-high heat and wipe it with the thinnest film of oil.
Pour about 1/3 cup batter near one edge and immediately swirl the pan or use the back of a flat spreader to sweep it into the thinnest possible layer.
Cook without flipping until the top is dry and the sheet releases at the edges, roughly 30–90 seconds depending on thickness.
Lift onto a clean cloth and repeat, adjusting batter with water if the sheets are too thick. Stack only after steam has dissipated slightly.

name: Moroccan Harira
imageAlt: Bowl of traditional Moroccan harira soup
imageCredit: Photo: Kattusa24, Wikimedia Commons, released to the public domain
summary: Moroccan harira with tomatoes, chickpeas, lentils, celery, cilantro, parsley and vermicelli, lightly thickened at the finish.
lead: Tomato, pulses and herbs build a silky Moroccan soup whose place at the Ramadan table is as important as its ingredients.
about: Harira is a Moroccan tomato-based soup built from pulses, herbs and often meat, rice or vermicelli. A flour-and-water thickener called tedouira can give the broth its characteristic silky body. Meatless and meat versions both exist; this one uses a modest amount of lamb or beef while keeping chickpeas, lentils, tomato and fresh herbs prominent.
story: Morocco's national tourism office identifies harira as a typical Moroccan soup made from pulses, tomato, pasta and flour and specifically notes its traditional role during Ramadan. The soup is closely associated with breaking the fast, commonly alongside dates and sweets, though it is eaten outside Ramadan as well. Recipes vary substantially by family, city and region, especially in meat, grain, spice and thickness.
caveat: There is no single canonical harira. This home version follows a widely documented chickpea-lentil-tomato structure and uses tedouira sparingly so the soup is silky rather than gluey.
prepNotes: Use cooked chickpeas if time is tight
Traditional dried chickpeas work beautifully, but pre-cooked chickpeas make the timing more predictable.
Chop herbs generously
Cilantro and parsley are structural ingredients here, not decorative garnishes.
Add tedouira slowly
The flour slurry thickens quickly; stop as soon as the broth turns lightly creamy.
ingredients: 8 oz lamb or beef, cut in small dice, optional
1 large onion, grated or finely chopped
2 celery stalks with leaves, finely chopped
1/4 cup all-purpose flour whisked smooth with 3/4 cup water
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
Lemon wedges and dates, for serving
steps: Heat oil in a large pot over medium heat. Brown meat if using for 4–5 minutes, then add onion and celery and cook until softened.
Add ginger, turmeric, pepper and cinnamon and stir 30 seconds.
Add crushed tomatoes and tomato paste and cook 8 minutes until the tomato tastes concentrated rather than raw.
Add chickpeas, lentils, cilantro, parsley and water or stock. Bring to a simmer, partially cover and cook 40–50 minutes until lentils are tender.
Add broken vermicelli and simmer until tender, usually 5–8 minutes.
Whisk the flour slurry again, then stream it into the simmering soup while stirring continuously. Start with half and add more only as needed.
Checkpoint: the broth should become silky and lightly creamy while still flowing freely from a ladle. If it turns heavy, thin with hot water.
Simmer 5 more minutes, taste for salt and serve hot with lemon and dates if desired.
sources: Moroccan National Tourist Office — Food & Drink: Harira

name: Jamaican Ackee and Saltfish
imageAlt: Jamaican ackee and saltfish served on a plate
imageCredit: Photo: gailf548, Wikimedia Commons/Flickr, CC BY 2.0
summary: Jamaica's national dish of tender ackee folded with salt cod, onion, tomato, sweet pepper, thyme and Scotch bonnet.
lead: Creamy ackee and flakes of salt cod meet tomato, thyme, sweet pepper and Scotch bonnet in Jamaica's national dish.
about: Ackee and saltfish combines cooked ackee fruit with rehydrated salted cod and a sauté of onion, tomato, sweet pepper, thyme and chile. Properly prepared ackee is tender and buttery and must be folded gently so the lobes do not disintegrate. For home cooks outside Jamaica, commercially canned ackee is the safest and most practical starting point.
story: Visit Jamaica identifies ackee and saltfish as Jamaica's national dish and a favorite breakfast, commonly served with dumplings, callaloo, green bananas, avocado or plantains. The dish brings together ackee, a fruit with West African origins, and preserved cod tied to Atlantic trade and colonial food systems; Jamaicans transformed those ingredients into a distinct national preparation. Its status today is both everyday and emblematic.
caveat: Unripe or improperly prepared fresh ackee can be dangerous. This recipe uses commercially canned ackee only. Never improvise with closed, unripe fresh ackee fruit.
prepNotes: Desalt the cod to taste
Saltfish brands vary. Soaking and a brief boil give you control over how much salt remains.
Drain canned ackee gently
Rinse minimally and let it drain without crushing the delicate lobes.
Fold, don't stir
Once ackee enters the pan, use a broad spatula and gentle turns to keep the pieces intact.
ingredients: 1/2 Scotch bonnet pepper, minced, or a larger piece left whole for less heat
Fried dumplings, boiled green banana, callaloo or plantain, for serving
steps: Soak salt cod in cool water for several hours or overnight, changing the water at least once. For a faster method, cover with fresh water and simmer 15–20 minutes, then drain and taste.
When the fish is pleasantly salty rather than harsh, remove skin or bones as needed and flake it into bite-size pieces.
Heat oil in a wide skillet over medium heat. Cook onion, bell peppers and scallions 4–5 minutes until softened but still colorful.
Add tomato, thyme and Scotch bonnet and cook 3 minutes.
Add saltfish and black pepper and sauté 3–4 minutes so the fish picks up the aromatics.
Add drained ackee and fold gently through the pan with a broad spatula.
Checkpoint: ackee should be hot through and coated with aromatics while the yellow lobes remain mostly intact rather than turning to mash.
Remove thyme stems and any whole chile piece. Serve immediately with Jamaican breakfast sides or ground provisions.
sources: Visit Jamaica — How to Make Ackee and Saltfish
Visit Jamaica — Jamaican Food and the national dish

name: Georgian Badrijani Nigvzit
imageAlt: Georgian eggplant with walnut filling and pomegranate seeds
imageCredit: Wikimedia Commons contributor, photographed in Georgia, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Thin eggplant slices wrapped around a garlicky Georgian walnut filling with coriander, vinegar and pomegranate.
lead: Silky eggplant wrapped around sharp, herby walnut paste—one of Georgia's classic walnut-and-vegetable combinations.
about: Badrijani nigvzit is Georgian eggplant with walnuts: thin slices of eggplant are fried or baked, then filled or spread with seasoned walnut paste. Garlic, coriander and vinegar sharpen the nuts, while pomegranate seeds often provide a fresh, tart garnish. The dish is typically served cool or at room temperature as part of a larger table.
story: Georgia's official tourism site describes eggplant with walnuts as a dish made in nearly every region of Georgia and served at supra tables. It belongs to a much larger Georgian tradition of combining vegetables with ground walnuts, herbs and acid—the same pantry logic that appears across pkhali and other cold dishes. Household forms vary from rolled spirals to folded slices and flat layered presentations.
caveat: Frying is common, but baking the eggplant is also documented and reduces oil absorption. This home recipe uses a skillet method with restrained oil and a traditional-style walnut filling.
prepNotes: Slice lengthwise and evenly
About 1/4 inch gives enough structure to roll without staying tough.
Salt before frying
A short salting draws surface moisture from the eggplant and helps it brown more predictably.
Do not turn walnuts into butter
Pulse finely but stop before the nuts release enough oil to become a paste on their own.
ingredients: 1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
1/4 tsp cayenne or red chile powder
3 tbsp white wine vinegar, plus more to taste
steps: Slice eggplants lengthwise about 1/4 inch thick. Sprinkle lightly with salt and rest 20 minutes, then blot dry.
Heat a thin layer of oil in a wide skillet over medium heat. Cook eggplant slices in batches until soft and golden on both sides, adding small amounts of oil as needed. Drain on towels or a rack.
Pulse walnuts, garlic, coriander, blue fenugreek, chile and a pinch of salt until very finely ground.
Add vinegar and enough water to make a thick, spreadable walnut mixture. Fold in cilantro.
Checkpoint: the filling should hold its shape on a spoon but spread without tearing the eggplant. Adjust with water by teaspoons if too stiff.
Spread about 1 tablespoon filling across each cooled eggplant slice and either fold in half or roll loosely.
Arrange on a platter and garnish with pomegranate seeds. Rest at least 20 minutes before serving so walnut, garlic and vinegar meld.
sources: Georgia Travel — A Guide to Vegetarian Georgian Food: Eggplant with Walnuts

name: Sri Lankan Pol Sambol
imageAlt: Traditional Sri Lankan pol sambol coconut relish
imageCredit: Photo: Dan arndt, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Fresh coconut pounded with red chile, red onion, lime and salt into Sri Lanka's vivid everyday pol sambol.
lead: Fresh coconut, chile, onion and lime become the sharp, bright relish that can wake up an entire Sri Lankan plate.
about: Pol sambol is a Sri Lankan coconut relish made from grated coconut, chile, onion, lime and salt, with Maldive fish included in many non-vegetarian versions. It is eaten with rice and curry, hoppers, string hoppers, bread and other staples. Good pol sambol should be moist and cohesive but still recognizably grated coconut, not a smooth puree.
story: Sri Lanka Tourism highlights pol sambol repeatedly in its culinary materials, describing coconut sambol as a traditional accompaniment and noting coconut's central place in the island's cooking. Regional and household versions vary in chile, Maldive fish and grinding method. Traditionally the ingredients may be worked on a miris gala grinding stone, where pressure bruises the onion and chile into the coconut rather than merely tossing separate ingredients together.
caveat: Freshly grated mature coconut gives the best texture. Unsweetened frozen coconut is the closest practical substitute; dry desiccated coconut needs light rehydration and will remain less juicy.
prepNotes: Use unsweetened coconut
Sweetened baking coconut is not suitable for this savory relish.
Crush before adding lime
Working chile, salt and onion into the coconut releases oils and creates a cohesive mixture.
Lime goes last
Acid brightens the sambol, but too much liquid can make the coconut soggy.
ingredients: 2 cups freshly grated mature coconut or thawed unsweetened frozen coconut
1 small red onion or 3 shallots, minced very finely
1 to 2 tbsp Sri Lankan red chile powder or crushed dried chile, to taste
1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
1 tbsp finely flaked Maldive fish, optional
steps: Combine coconut, onion, chile, salt and Maldive fish if using in a mortar, on a grinding stone or in a wide bowl.
Pound and press the mixture for several minutes rather than simply stirring. If using a bowl, rub small handfuls firmly between your fingers.
Checkpoint: the coconut should begin to clump lightly, with red chile distributed evenly and the raw edge of the onion softened by bruising.
Add 2 tablespoons lime juice and mix thoroughly.
Taste a full spoonful. Add additional chile, salt or lime until the sambol is hot, salty and bright while still tasting clearly of coconut.
Serve immediately or at room temperature with rice, dhal, hoppers, string hoppers or bread.
sources: Sri Lanka Tourism — Culinary Tourism: Coconut Sambal / Pol Sambola
Sri Lanka Tourism — Cuisine and pol sambol
Central Province Tourism Department — Sri Lankan cuisine and pol sambol

name: Lao Tam Mak Hoong
imageAlt: Lao-style green papaya salad tam mak hoong served in Luang Prabang
imageCredit: Photo: Jpatokal, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Lao green papaya salad pounded with garlic, chile, long beans, tomato, lime and deeply savory padaek.
lead: Crunchy green papaya bruised just enough to drink in chile, lime and fermented fish—the Lao pounded salad in its own right.
about: Tam mak hoong is Lao green papaya salad. Shredded unripe papaya is bruised in a mortar with garlic, chile, long beans, tomato and a savory-sour dressing. Padaek, Lao fermented fish sauce, is a defining ingredient in many versions and gives the Lao salad a deeper fermented character than sweeter neighboring forms.
story: Pha Khao Lao describes tam mak hoong as both a snack and part of a meal and stresses that the balance is highly personal: some versions are sweeter or sourer, while regional salads can use crab paste or other local fermented seasonings. The method matters as much as the formula. The mortar should bruise and season the papaya, not crush it into wet pulp. Sticky rice commonly accompanies the salad and helps balance its chile and fermented intensity.
caveat: Padaek can be pungent and varies by producer. Use a commercially prepared product intended for ready-to-eat seasoning, or substitute standard fish sauce with the understanding that the flavor becomes cleaner and less distinctly Lao.
prepNotes: Use truly green papaya
Ripe papaya is sweet and soft and cannot provide the required crisp texture.
Pound in stages
Garlic and chile need more force than papaya and tomato. Add delicate ingredients later.
Keep the papaya crunchy
Once strands soften slightly and absorb dressing, stop. More pounding is not better.
ingredients: 1 small green papaya, peeled, seeded and shredded into about 5 cups strands
2 to 5 fresh bird's eye chiles, to taste
2 tsp palm or brown sugar, plus more to taste
1 1/2 tbsp padaek or 1 tbsp fish sauce
1/2 tsp shrimp or crab paste, optional
steps: Pound garlic, chiles and salt in a large mortar until broken into a coarse paste.
Add sugar, padaek, lime juice and shrimp or crab paste if using. Pound and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Add long beans and pound 4–5 times to bruise them while keeping distinct pieces.
Add tomatoes and press gently with the pestle just until they release some juice.
Add shredded papaya in two or three additions, using a spoon to lift strands from the bottom while the pestle lightly bruises from above.
Checkpoint: papaya should bend more easily and look glossy with dressing but remain crisp and separate, never mashed.
Taste for the balance you prefer—salty-fermented, hot and sour, with sweetness in a supporting role. Adjust lime, padaek, chile or sugar and serve immediately with sticky rice.
sources: Pha Khao Lao — Tam Mak Hoong / Papaya Salad
